Best,
Erin

messages.subject: Re: 3-option probabilistic reversal learning
messages.body_plain:
Hi Erin,

Thanks for your interest!

It would probably be best to start off with a model like the 3-armed bandit that was posted on the forum earlier, and then you could work your way up to trying more complex models that have a reversal learning component. One model that may be useful in your case would be a 3-armed bandit with a pearce hall rule. The pearce hall rule tends to capture reversal learning pretty well. We do not have this model in hBayesDM at the moment, but here is an example application if you are interested in implementing it yourself: http://cosanlab.com/static/papers/Taylor_2017_Pain.pdf

I hope this helps! Let us know if you have any other questions.

Best,

Nate

Hi Wojciech,

I think this is all a function of these choice RT models requiring many observations to get accurate parameter estimates. Before continuing, I think it would be best to simulate more than 500 trials (e.g. 2000 or more is probably best) and checking if you can recover parameters from those data. I think that with only 500 trials for a single subject, the data are not offering strong enough evidence to shift the priors by much. In this case, the posteriors are so wide that the mean does not give much information.

That said, recovery tends to work much better with fewer trials when there are multiple subjects. I have attached an image here showing the results of a parameter recovery that I ran on the LBA with 5 subjects worth of data (500 trials per condition). You can see that the extreme estimates get pulled toward the group averages, but overall the models recover the ranking of the parameters well.

Anyway, I hope this helps. Let me know if you still get strange results with more simulated data.

Best,

Nate

Hi Wojciech,

Thanks a lot for the detailed analysis!

After running things on my machine, however, I am getting much different results. I have attached a screenshot (and R script) here showing that the relative magnitudes of the drift rates can be recovered just fine.

I found that if I simulate data multiple times (with the same parameters) and refit the simulated data, I get much different drift rates (e.g., sometimes the means are opposite to what it should be like in your case) each time. I attached an R script here with the rng seed that I used so you can replicate my results. I think this is due to the choiceRT models being difficult to identify, as I mentioned previously. You will get more consistent results with more trials and more separated drift rates (e.g., mean_v = c(3,1)).

As for the multiple subject data, did you write the data out as tab separated? The help files specify that all .txt files should be tab separated to be read in correctly.

Best,
Nate
